title: Standing waves and harmonics
summary: Find a string's pitch, see how the pluck point picks the harmonics, and hear why a ruler doesn't sound like a guitar.

steps.title: The fundamental
steps.text:
A string fixed at both ends vibrates in standing waves. The lowest, the fundamental, has frequency

    f₁ = c / 2L,   c = √(T / ρ)

For this guitar string (65 cm, 70 N, 0.6 g/m) that is about 263 Hz, middle C. Run it and read the Fundamental frequency in the Summary.

check.success: 262.7 Hz: c = 342 m/s over twice the length.

steps.title: Where you pluck matters
steps.text: The overtones of a string are harmonics: 2f₁, 3f₁, … How strongly each one sounds depends on where you pluck. Pluck exactly in the middle and run: the Mode content tab shows that the even modes are missing, because the middle is a node (a point that never moves) of every even mode.

check.hint: Set the position to 0.5 and run.
check.success: No second harmonic: a middle pluck sounds hollow.

steps.title: Missing the fifth
steps.text: Now pluck at one fifth of the length (Position 0.2). Which mode goes missing this time? Run and check the Mode content tab.

check.success: Mode 5 has a node at L/5, so plucking there cannot excite it (nor modes 10, 15, …).

steps.title: A ruler is not a guitar
steps.text: A ruler hanging over a table edge is a cantilever beam. It resists through bending stiffness instead of tension, so its overtones are not whole multiples of the fundamental. Run the ruler and look at f2 / f1 in the Summary and the Mode shapes tab.

check.success: 6.27, not 2: that is why a twanged ruler buzzes rather than rings.

steps.title: Damping
steps.text: Real strings lose energy. Back on the guitar string, set the damping ratio to 2 % and run: the Energy tab shows the vibration dying away.

check.success: Most of the energy is gone within a few hundredths of a second.
